scenes.visual: Title card 'Same Warmth, Two Answers' over two empty climate-diagram frames side by side, labelled 'station A' and 'station B'. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: RED line = monthly temperature; BLUE line = monthly rain; GOLD shading = a dry month; BLUE parcel = moist rising air; GOLD parcel = dry sinking air; GREEN = forest; TAN = desert or dry grass. Cream background, 16:9. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Globes, parcels, trees and torches are simple cartoons labelled 'schematic'; climate-diagram lines and sunlight bars are computed from the lesson's numbers and labelled 'computed'.

scenes.tts: The first film built a rule. Rain falls where moist air rises, and warmer months need more rain to count as humid.
scenes.visual: Brief recap: the first film's globe with its rising BLUE parcel and sinking GOLD parcel, then its rule card with three lines. The card shrinks into the corner and stays there.
scenes.narration: The first film built a rule. Rain falls where moist air rises, and warmer months need more rain to count as humid.

scenes.tts: Now test it on two made-up stations. Both average about twenty-six degrees. What grows at each?
scenes.caption: Now test it on two made-up stations. Both average about 26 °C. What grows at each?
scenes.visual: Two station pins on a tropical lowland cartoon, labelled 'station A' and 'station B (made-up data)'. Under each, a RED temperature line draws in; on-screen label 'average about 26 °C' under both.
scenes.narration: Now test it on two made-up stations. Both average about 26 °C. What grows at each?

scenes.tts: Station A is the one you just worked. Its blue rain line rides above the red in every month.
scenes.visual: Station A's computed diagram: RED line flat at 26 degrees C (the 52 mm level); BLUE line through 140, 120, 150, 180, 200, 160, 140, 110, 90, 100, 130, 160 mm, always above. On-screen total '1,680 mm a year' (computed).
scenes.narration: Station A is the one you just worked. Its blue rain line rides above the red in every month.

scenes.tts: No month is dry. Its class letters are A and F: tropical, with no dry month. That is a tropical rainforest climate.
scenes.caption: No month is dry. Its class is Af: tropical, with no dry month. That is a tropical rainforest climate.
scenes.visual: A green tick over the diagram, label 'no dry month'. A badge 'Af, tropical rainforest climate' appears; a GREEN closed-canopy cartoon grows behind station A.
scenes.narration: No month is dry. Its class is Af: tropical, with no dry month. That is a tropical rainforest climate.

scenes.tts: Station B has the same average warmth, though its months run from about twenty-four to thirty degrees. But it gets about two thirds as much rain, and most of it falls from April to October.
scenes.caption: Station B has the same average warmth, though its months run from about 24 to 30 °C. But it gets about two thirds as much rain, and most of it falls from April to October.
scenes.visual: Station B's computed diagram: RED line between 24 and 30 degrees C; BLUE line through 5, 10, 30, 80, 150, 180, 200, 220, 160, 60, 15, 5 mm. On-screen totals: '1,115 mm' beside station A's '1,680 mm' (computed).
scenes.narration: Station B has the same average warmth, though its months run from about 24 to 30 °C. But it gets about two thirds as much rain, and most of it falls from April to October.

scenes.tts: From November to March, the blue line drops below the red. Those five months fill with gold. They are the dry season.
scenes.visual: Under station B's RED line, the gaps for January, February, March, November and December fill GOLD one by one, with a counter '5 dry months'. April to October stay clear.
scenes.narration: From November to March, the blue line drops below the red. Those five months fill with gold. They are the dry season.

scenes.tts: Its class letters are A and W: tropical, with a marked dry season. That is a tropical savanna climate. The rule's first guess is grass with scattered trees.
scenes.caption: Its class is Aw: tropical, with a marked dry season. That is a tropical savanna climate. The rule's first guess is grass with scattered trees.
scenes.visual: Badge 'Aw, tropical savanna climate' appears. A TAN grassland with a few scattered tree cartoons grows behind station B, labelled 'first guess'.
scenes.narration: Its class is Aw: tropical, with a marked dry season. That is a tropical savanna climate. The rule's first guess is grass with scattered trees.

scenes.tts: So far the rule gives two first guesses. Similar warmth, different rain, different climate classes. Now look at station B's rain once more.
scenes.visual: Both diagrams side by side with their badges, 'Af, first guess: forest' and 'Aw, first guess: savanna'. Then station B's total '1,115 mm' enlarges and glows.
scenes.narration: So far the rule gives two first guesses. Similar warmth, different rain, different climate classes. Now look at station B's rain once more.

scenes.tts: Staver, Archibald and Levin analysed tree cover across the tropics. They looked at places with about a thousand to two and a half thousand millimetres of rain a year.
scenes.caption: Staver, Archibald and Levin analysed tree cover across the tropics. They looked at places with about 1,000 to 2,500 mm of rain a year.
scenes.visual: Name card 'Staver, Archibald and Levin, 2011'. A horizontal rain axis appears with a shaded window from 1,000 to 2,500 mm a year, and a second label 'dry season shorter than 7 months'.
scenes.narration: Staver, Archibald and Levin analysed tree cover across the tropics. They looked at places with about 1,000 to 2,500 mm of rain a year.

scenes.tts: Those places also had a dry season shorter than seven months, by the study's own measure. There, tree cover was rarely in between. Places were mostly savanna, or mostly forest.
scenes.visual: Above the window, a schematic two-humped bar chart of tree cover (x axis 'tree cover, low to high'): a tall TAN hump at low cover and a tall GREEN hump at high cover, a gap between. Labelled 'schematic of the reported pattern' and, under the 7-month label, 'dry season measured the study's way'. No station pin yet.
scenes.narration: Those places also had a dry season shorter than seven months, by the study's own measure. There, tree cover was rarely in between. Places were mostly savanna, or mostly forest.

scenes.tts: Station B's rain total falls in that range, and its diagram points to savanna. Would every place with a climate like that be savanna?
scenes.visual: Station B's pin drops onto the rain axis at 1,115 mm, inside the shaded rainfall range (its dry-month count is not shown against the 7-month label). Beside it, station B's diagram with the 'Aw' badge and an empty landscape outline with a question mark: 'always savanna?'
scenes.narration: Station B's rain total falls in that range, and its diagram points to savanna. Would every place with a climate like that be savanna?

scenes.visual: Hold; a timer ring fills over five seconds.

scenes.tts: No. In that window, savanna and forest were both found under similar climates. And fire was associated with keeping areas open.
scenes.visual: The empty outline splits into two patches under one generic climate-summary card ('similar rain total and season'): left, TAN grass with scattered trees; right, a GREEN closed canopy. Label: 'similar climates, two states (observed across the tropics)'.
scenes.narration: No. In that window, savanna and forest were both found under similar climates. And fire was associated with keeping areas open.

scenes.tts: Where grass is open, fire can keep it open. A closed canopy can hold fire back. So each state may help keep itself going.
scenes.visual: Left patch: an orange fire line sweeps across the grass in a GOLD dry month and the scattered trees stay few. Right patch: the same fire line reaches the canopy edge and fades out. Labels: 'fire can keep open areas open' and 'a closed canopy can hold fire back' (schematic; strength varies from place to place).
scenes.narration: Where grass is open, fire can keep it open. A closed canopy can hold fire back. So each state may help keep itself going.

scenes.tts: This is a pattern, not proof. Savanna and forest may be alternative states under similar climates. Whether those states are truly stable is still debated.
scenes.visual: Caption card 'association, not proven cause'. The two patches sit on either side of a gentle hill outline, a ball resting in each valley (schematic), with a small question mark over the hill top labelled 'stable? still debated'.
scenes.narration: This is a pattern, not proof. Savanna and forest may be alternative states under similar climates. Whether those states are truly stable is still debated.

scenes.tts: So climate gives a first guess at the biome. Fire, soils, the timing of rain and microclimate can change the answer. A savanna climate does not guarantee a savanna.
scenes.visual: The rule card from the corner returns, and four tags attach beneath it: 'fire', 'soils', 'rain timing', 'microclimate'. Station A and station B diagrams sit below.
scenes.narration: So climate gives a first guess at the biome. Fire, soils, the timing of rain and microclimate can change the answer. A savanna climate does not guarantee a savanna.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Climate gives a first guess at a biome, not the answer.'
